title: Set the Onboarding SLA Policy
subtitle: Deadlines in business days before the start date
scenario: It is SD-5. Before the plan can assign due dates, Harbor needs an agreed SLA policy - written once, owned, and versioned - so no provisioning task invents its own deadline. Record each task's deadline as business days before the start date.
input: People Ops has agreed onboarding service levels, measured in business days before the start date (SD). Payroll must be enrolled earliest - 3 business days before start (SD-3) - so the hire lands in the first pay cycle. Accounts are due 2 business days before (SD-2). Hardware and building/system access are due 1 business day before (SD-1). The policy is owned by the People Ops Lead and changes are versioned. Record this as version 1.0.0.
instructions: Read the SLA brief and note each task's deadline in business days before start.
Set accountsSla, hardwareSla, accessSla, and payrollSla as plain numbers (days before SD).
Record the policy name, owner, and a version.
Payroll is earliest, so payrollSla must be greater than accountsSla, then validate.
copilotPrompt: Draft a JSON onboarding SLA policy with policyName, version, owner, and four deadlines as plain numbers of business days before start: accountsSla, hardwareSla, accessSla, payrollSla. Make payroll the earliest (largest days before start).
successMessage: SLA policy set and versioned. The provisioning plan can now stamp each task with an owned deadline instead of a guess.
editorHelper: Write the deadlines once, as owned config every task reads.

intro.heading: Before you plan: what 'on time' means

sections.title: SLAs are fields, not folklore
sections.body: How early each task must finish is a governed value, not something each provisioner remembers differently. Writing it down once means the plan and the gate apply the same deadlines.

sections.title: Relative to the start date
sections.body: Every deadline is measured backward from SD - the start date. SD-3 means three business days before. Store the number of days so the plan can compute a real due date from any hire's start.

sections.title: Payroll leads for a reason
sections.body: Payroll is due earliest (SD-3) because enrollment has to land before the first pay cycle. Ordering the deadlines encodes that dependency: payroll before accounts before the day-of tasks.

sections.title: Owned and versioned
sections.body: The People Ops Lead owns the policy and every change is versioned. A shorter SLA buys margin before day one but strains the provisioning teams - so the number is a governed decision.

takeaway.heading: SLA policy set
points: You recorded each task's deadline as business days before the start date.
Payroll leads (SD-3) so enrollment lands before the first pay cycle - the ordering is deliberate.
The People Ops Lead owns the policy and it is versioned, so deadlines are governed, not guessed.
The plan can now stamp every task with a real due date derived from the hire's start.
The workflow can now say what 'on time' means for every provisioning task.
